Dr. Sumudu Premachandra J.
1] The Accused Appellant is charged with a single offence of grave sexual abuse
from the period of 01/05/2018 to 05/10/2018 under Section 365 B (2) (b) of
the Penal Code.
2] The evidences show that the Accused, who was known to the Victim as
“Suresh Aiya” and was the partner of her elder sister, sexually abused the
approximately 12-year-old Victim while she was alone at home and
subsequently threatened to kill her mother and sister if she disclosed the
incident. The Victim (PW 01) remained silent because of these threats and later
attempted to leave home, intending to travel towards Galle to become a Buddhist
nun. Then, her Grade 7 teacher was informed by peer students that she is going
to Galle after school. The teacher noticed her distressed condition following
which she took victim to her sister and the victim disclosed the incident to her
sister and mother. A complaint was made to the Nawagattegama Police on
06/10/2018, and the Accused was arrested on 07/10/2018, in Marawila. The
Prosecution relied principally on the evidence of PW 01, PW 02, and PW 10, the
class teacher, the Victim’s birth certificate and Medico Legal Report (P1 and P2),
the evidence of the Judicial Medical Officer, and the police investigation.
3] The Defence challenged the Prosecution case by relying on inconsistencies
and omissions in the Victim’s statements and other details of the incident. The
Defence also relied on the Victim’s admission that she had previously made an
untruthful allegation concerning another person, the mother’s differing
accounts of when she first learned of the abuse, the Victim’s inability to identify
the precise date of the offence, the delay in making the complaint, and the
absence of significant physical or forensic evidence. The JMO examination found
no tears or injuries to the hymen or external genitalia, but the medical evidence
diagnosed the Victim with severe psychological distress. The Prosecution
explained the delay by reference to the threats made against the Victim and the
psychological trauma arising from them.
4] After a contested trial, the Appellant was convicted for the charge and
sentenced to 8 years’ rigorous imprisonment. In addition, Rs.10,000/- fine
imposed and Rs.200,000/- compensation is to be paid to the Victim, in default
3 months and 1-year simple imprisonment were imposed respectively.
5] Being aggrieved to the said conviction and sentence, the Appellant prefers this
appeal on the following grounds;
1. The Learned High Court Judge has erred in law in regard to the burden of
proof and the quantum of proof.
2. The overall approach of the Learned High Court Judge followed in the
analysis and evaluation of evidence is contrary to the law.
3. The Learned High Court Judge had failed to appreciate that PW 01 is not
a trustworthy witness.
4. The Learned High Court Judge had failed to appreciate that the
Prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
5. The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by severing portions from the
evidence of PW 01 and the other witnesses called by the Prosecution and
holding that such witnesses are trustworthy.
6. The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the Medico Legal
Report and evidence of the Medical Officer also contradict the evidence of
PW 01.
7. The Learned High Court Judge erred in law in rejecting the dock statement
of the Accused on behalf of the Defence.
8. The Learned High Court Judge has erred in law and facts.
6] When considering the evidence of PW 01, she was 12 years old at the incident,
however, in a short history she has mentioned she is 13 years old. She has
testified at the age of 17 years. It is seen that she had clearly testified what
happened to her at the time of the incident. She said the Accused came in a
motorbike on the particular date; he was in a blue shirt. He asked for a glass of
water and when she brought the glass of water, she had seen that the front door
was closed by the accused. Then she was dragged to a bed and he placed his
penis on her vagina. Thus, the act is clearly expressed by the Victim.
7] To the belatedness, she said that the Accused threatened to kill the mother
and elder sister. Moreover, she had mentioned at the testimony, the Accused
coached if this incident accidently slipped off her tongue, tell it was not the truth.
Thus, it is superficially seen that the evidence of the PW 01, the Victim, tally
with the other Witnesses’ evidence.
8] The learned Trial Judge had, in assessing the evidence, applied the principles
in Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v State of Gujarat AIR 1983 753, Banda v Attorney
General (1999) 3 SLR 168, and Dharmasiri v Republic (2012) 1 SLR 268,
recognizing that minor inconsistencies do not necessarily undermine credible
testimony when the central narrative remains intact.
9] The Defence principally challenged the credibility and reliability of PW 01 and
the other Prosecution Witnesses, relying on substantial contradictions and
omissions between PW 01’s evidence in court and her original police statement,
marked as V-01 to V-05. These included inconsistencies concerning how the
Accused entered the house, whether PW 01’s mouth was covered, whether she
screamed, and the nature of the alleged physical injuries. The Defence further
relied on the evidence of the Judicial Medical Officer (PW 07), who found no fresh
or old injuries, no genital trauma and no physical signs of forcible penetration,
and no medical evidence directly connecting PW 01’s medical condition or
adjustment disorder with the alleged assault. PW 03’s evidence was also
challenged because she initially referred to an unknown offender before
subsequently implicating the Accused.
10] The Defence additionally relied on evidence from PW 10, PW 01’s teacher,
concerning alleged scolding, physical punishment and family pressure at home,
together with alleged prior animosity and police complaints between the Accused
and PW 01’s family, as circumstances supporting the possibility of a false
implication.
11] In support of the appeal, the Learned Counsel for the Defence argued that
the Prosecution failed to establish the charge beyond reasonable doubt,
emphasizing that the burden of proof remained entirely with the Prosecution
and that the Accused was not required to prove his innocence.
12] I now consider the merits of the case. Article 13 (5) of the Constitution (Every
person shall be presumed innocent until he is proved guilty: Provided that the
burden of proving particular facts may, by law, be placed on an Accused person)
norms that the court should draw the presumption of innocence until guilty of
the Accused is proved and this provision enriched by Article 13 (3) (Article 13(3)
Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or
by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.) enabling the right
to represent by an attorney at law and by giving fair trial. The golden rule in
criminal law is that the burden is on the Prosecution to prove guilty of the
Accused. Thus, the ingredients of the charge must be proved.
13] in proving a fact, “Proved” or “Disproved” of a fact is defined in Section 3 of
the Evidence Ordinance. It defines what is meant by proved and disproved. It
says;
“A fact is said to be proved when, after considering all the matters before it,
the Court either believes it to exist or considers its existence so probable
that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the
particular case, to act upon the supposition that it exists.
A fact is said to be disproved when, after considering the matters before it,
the Court either believes that it does not exist, or considers its non-
existence so probable that a prudent man ought, under the
circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that
it does not exist. A fact is said not to be proved when it is neither proved nor
disproved.” [Emphasis is added]
14] Thus, the yardstick of existence of fact should be decided in the angle of
prudent man. The yardstick of the existence of a fact must be decided not by a
trained judicial mind such as judges or attorneys, must be by a prudent man
who is not a lunatic or mentally retarded who thinks in totality of evidence,
whether the fact is believed to be proved or not, whether the charge can be
sustained or not considering the totality of oral and documentary evidence which
came from the witness box; substantive evidence.
15] In Nandana Kumarage Sujeewa Nishanka Karunarathna vs Officer-in-
charge, Police Station, Rambukkana, SC APPEAL NO:
SC/APPEAL/61/2023, Decided on: 09/10/2024, His Lordship
Samayawardhena, J. held what is reasonable doubt as;
“The prosecution must prove the accused’s guilt beyond a “reasonable
doubt”, not beyond “any doubt”. A reasonable doubt refers to a doubt based
on logical reasoning through proper evaluation of evidence. This requires
the trier of fact to weigh all evidence supporting guilt against evidence
suggesting innocence, considering the strengths and weaknesses on both
sides. If, after this evaluation, the evidence overwhelmingly favors the
prosecution and eliminates any reasonable doubt about the guilt of the
accused, the case can be deemed proven beyond a reasonable doubt. This
standard applies to the totality of the evidence as a whole, not to each
individual piece of evidence the prosecution relies on to prove the guilt of the
accused.”
16] We are in a system of rules of evidence adopted by English Law. It should be
stressed that the case is decided by the evidence on oath by the witnesses
affirming telling the truth and nothing but the truth. Biblical verse John 19:35
says;
“The man who saw it, has given testimony, and his testimony is true. He
knows that he tells the truth, and he testifies, so that you also may
believe.”1
17] Hence, witnesses and their role in determining outcomes of cases are crucial
for trials in the courts. A favorable witness in providing favorable testimony
works for strengthening the case of the party producing that Witness. However,
it must be assessed not in isolation but as a whole and along with other
supportive evidence. We are being judges, State Counsels, Defense Counsels not
at the vicinity of the crime, it is the witness who tells the facts thus we have to
assess on the level of a prudent man whether the incident could happen or not.
18] In this trial the following contradictions were marked. In වී 1, the
contradiction was that “ඊට පසේ්සේ දැක්කා කළුපාට බයික් එකක් කුසේිය පැත්්ත් ජ්ේලය ළඟ
නවත්වලා ති්යනවා”. In her evidence, incident took around 1pm to 2pm, she had
opened the main door and was expecting someone. However, in the police
statement, she said, that she heard someone was walking near the side window
and then she opened the door and the Accused entered the house. Then, she
asked why he has come. This position was marked as වී 2 and it was “මම සු්ේෂේ
අය්යා්ෙේ ඇහුවා ඇයි ්ම් ේ ආ්ේ කියලා”. In the evidence, she denied any conversation
between the Accused and her. Then, in the police station she had told the
following as වී 3, “මම කෑෙැහුවා” and වී 4 as “මට ්ොඩක් රිදුණා. මම කෑෙැහුවා. කවුරුත් ආ්ේ
නැ ැ” and වී 5 as “ම්ේ චූ කරණ තැනයි , බඩයි ්ොඩක් රිදුණා”. The trial court had noted
the following omissions that “චුදිත්ේ අතිේ කට වැහුවා” and “්පාරවන ෂීට් එක විේදිත
තැනැත්තිය ස චුදිත යන ්ද්දනාම විිේ ්පාරවා ෙත බව”. In her police statement, she has
told that she screamed, but she denied at the testimony that she screamed but

no one had come. In the Police Statement, she said that she felt pain in the
vagina and groin. It is seen that the police statement was recorded before going
to the JMO. There were no injuries in the medical report. This part was not
supported by the medical evidence. Thus, evince in mainly contradicting the
police statement. The above contradictions mainly related to grave sexual abuse
and she said she did not feel pain at the testimony. The attention can be drawn
that if she felt pain in the vagina and groin that the Accused had penetrated her,
but medical report indicates otherwise.
19] It is further seen until the question was confronted, she had hidden there
was a previous incident not relating to grave sexual abuse by someone else. She
testified;
“ප්‍ර. ොල්්ල් ඉසේ්කෝ්ල් යන කා්ල් විදුෂි ට ්මානවා රි කරදරයක් ිද්ධ වුනාද කා්ෙේ රි ?
ප්‍ර. විදුෂි පාස්ල් ඉදේ කැ්ල්කට එක්කේ ගිහිල්ලා කරදරයක් වු්ේ නැද්ද?
උ. පාස්ල් ඉදේ නැ ැ. මම 01 වස්ේදී ව්ේ අය්යා ්ක්නක් කැ්ලකට ඇදේ ගියා . සීයා
තමයි ්ේරාෙත්්ත්.
ප්‍ර. දැේ මීට කලිේ කරදරයක් උ්ේ නැ ැ කියලා කිේ්ේ?
උ. එ්කේ කරදරයක් උ්ේ නැ ැ
ප්‍ර. කැ්ලට එක්කේ ගිය එක කරදරයක් ්නා්ේද විදුෂි ?
උ. ඔේ. ඊට පසේ්සේ සීයා තමයි එක්කේ ආ්ේ.
ප්‍ර. ඒක කරදරයක් ්ේද? උ. ඔේ”
20] Though, this fact may not be important to this incident, it revealed that the
Victim was not new to this situation and it question the reliability of the witness.
21] වී 6, contradiction was marked through the Victim’s sister. She has told the
police that the Victim did not reveal the perpetrator first and had told her
“අ න්කාට කිේවා ළමා සමා්ජට ගිහිේ එද්දී කරදරයක් උනා කියලා”. But, in her evidence, she
said the Victim directly told her that the perpetrator is the Accused “Suresh
Kumara”. This is major contradiction inter se.
22] Are the above contradictions material? A material contradiction is a
significant and irreconcilable inconsistency in a Witness's statements or
evidence that goes to the core of a legal case and creates reasonable doubt. It
involves with central facts such as the identity of the Accused, the core action
of a crime, or vital elements of a dispute rather than minor, peripheral details.
Unlike trivial discrepancies or normal human memory lapses, a material
contradiction severely undermines the reliability and truthfulness of a Witness.
In a trial, proving a material contradiction can lead to the rejection of a Witness's
testimony and may result in an acquittal or a ruling in favour of the Accused.
23] In a material contradiction two statements flatly oppose each other on a
crucial point. There is a small variation in the details, such as a slight
miscalculation of time or a minor difference in description, which courts usually
accept as normal human fallibility. In this case all contradictions are involved
with major acts. The door was closed, but in the evidence, the door was open,
she felt a pain in the vagina and groin. But in evidence she said no pain was
caused in line with non-penetration. It should be noted that the evidence should
consider inter se and per se with other evidence. The Victim cannot be held as
a tender child who does not know the physical act. She was 12 years’ and had
already attended puberty at the time of the incident. The learned trial judge had
failed to consider the Accused was the sister’s partner and she had a child from
him. The Accused was underage and the sister did not consent to marry him.
The sister suspected the Accused had other affairs. However, the Accused
wanted to be with her. Thus, the Accused was pestering the sister. In her
mother’s statement, the sister was admitted to the mental hospital over these
incidents. Thus, she was not normal. Thus, her mental behaviour is volatile.
Further, the learned trial judge also failed to consider that the Victim told PW
10, the teacher who found her at the bus stand that she wanted to become a
Buddhist nun, because of extensive pressure of the Victim’s mother and elder
sister. This is inter se contradiction between two witnesses. It is a fact, the
Victim’s family complained against the Accused to the Nawagattegama Police
two times previously. One prudent man can think, that they wanted the Accused
to be out of the scene. In the light of the above, I am of the view that the above
contradictions must be assessed, in view of the prudent man, not on the trained
judicial mind.
24] It is to be noted that the state must prove every element of a charge beyond
a reasonable doubt. If a contradiction shakes the core of the proof, a logical and
sensible doubt arises, the judge must give the Accused the benefit of the doubt
as a matter of right, leading to a not-guilty verdict.
25] In the case in hand, there was a single act, thus the Victim cannot be
jumbled with any previous sexual acts. If the Victim is subjected to continuous
or few more sexual assaults a prudent man can believe she may have jumbled
with a previous act. But if it is a single act, there cannot be any mess with the
evidence. Thus, I consider that the learned trial judge ought to have considered
the contradictions in favor of the accused in the back drop of the case, at her
conclusion. It is to be noted that direct evidence can be concocted without a
single contradiction when the Witnesses get together and make up a story. In
such circumstances, it is a trial judge’s bounded duty to consider the
background of the story. In this case, the scene of the crime was shown by the
sister not by the Victim “්මම අපරාධ සේථානය දැරිය්ේ ්සා් ායුරිය වන රුවනි ම් ේෂිකා්ේ
මෙ ්පේවීම යට්ත් ්සායාෙත්තා.” The Accused was the paramour of Ruwani
Maheshika, who was underage and pestering them. She had shown the scene of
crime, if she was not there at the material time, how can she show the place?
Thus, in applying the prudent man’s test, one can think the story may have
concocted to remove the Accused from the scene. Thus, this benefit of doubt is
reasonable and must be given to the Accused. Thus, I hold the conviction is
unsafe.
26] In Ambika Prasad v State of New Delhi, 2000 SCC CRL 522, Indian
Supreme Court held;
“A criminal trial is meant for doing justice to the accused, victim and society.
So that law and order is maintained. A judge does not preside over a
criminal trial merely to see that no innocent man is punished. A judge also
presides to see that a guilty man does not escape. One is as important as
the other. Both are public duties.”
27] For the reasons stated above, I set aside the conviction and the sentence
dated 11/09/2025. The Accused Appellant is acquitted and discharged.
The appeal is allowed.

AMAL RANARAJA J.
